Trump called AI concerns “a HOAX.”

He said opponents of data centers “want to end up being backwards and poor.”
No, Mr. President, Americans want Congress and you to do your job protecting humanity, protecting our utility bills, and protecting us from out-of-control, corrupt greed.

A principal role for government is to protect the American people. Safety must always be our first mandate. It is also the government’s job to protect the American people from unmitigated greed. The billionaires that you are listening to now would prefer the government stay on the sidelines. But the U.S. government knows how to regulate corporate greed and how to address new technologies that could destroy our world.

The robber barons of the Gilded Age amassed enormous fortunes while working families struggled. Soon thereafter, unchecked Wall Street speculation and a devastating stock market crash helped plunge America into the Great Depression.

President Franklin D. Roosevelt and Democrats responded with landmark reforms to rein in Wall Street, protect working families, and prevent another financial catastrophe. They established the Securities and Exchange Commission to police the stock market, created Social Security to provide economic security for Americans, and enacted the first federal minimum wage to protect workers from exploitation.

When we invented and exploded the atomic bomb in New Mexico in 1944, the scientist who oversaw it, J. Robert Oppenheimer, said, “now I am become Death, the destroyer of worlds.” He realized that this new technology could mean the end of humankind. After Hiroshima and Nagasaki, the United States, Congress, and our top scientists worked to limit the spread of nuclear weapons, even while many of the scientific inventions coming out of that discovery made their way into our business community and way of life.

What we do now will matter. We cannot just let AI and data centers regulate themselves or depend on their goodwill to lower utility costs and limit the most destructive possibilities inherent in this rapidly evolving technology. We must let local communities have a say in what is built in their neighborhoods so they can protect their water, environment, and cost burdens. 

But Congress must act. There must be a strong, enforceable national regulatory framework. We must have civil and criminal liability. We must protect the local and national financial interests of working families.

It is not a hoax, Mr. President. And we have a job to do.

Emmett Till was robbed of his life but also of his own unique Black future. And to remember him is to honor not only the life stolen from him, but the one he deserved to live.

This weekend, I visited "If Emmett Till Lived," the powerful new exhibition in Chicago that affirms the fullness of the man he could have become.

I was honored to select a work of art and contribute a reflection for this exhibit, and it was a joy to spend time with the visionary @sarahelizalewis and Rev. Wheeler Parker Jr., Emmett's cousin, best friend, and last surviving witness to his kidnapping, who helped bring it to life.

For the first time, I invoked Emmett Till's name and didn't feel heaviness. Instead, I was immersed in blissful opportunities to imagine him as a father, a husband, and a Black man who loved softball and dreamed of being a police officer.

While the strange fruit of Black bodies hang from trees across America and Black history is under attack, exhibitions like these are a necessary reminder not only of America's legacy of lynching and racial terror—but also of the Black futures that are lost when Black lives are stolen.

It's why I'll continue demanding a thorough, transparent, and comprehensive federal investigation into the suspicious deaths of Black folks found hanging across the country, as authorized by the Emmett Till Antilynching Act of 2022.

It's why I'll continue defending Black history and our museums—including the Smithsonian and other cultural institutions—from the unprecedented, anti-Black, and fascist assault from the occupant of the White House.

And it's why I'll always fight for Black lives, Black families, Black futures, and our collective liberation.

"If Emmett Till Lived" will be on display until December 19th and you can check it out at the Museum of Contemporary Photography on S Michigan Ave in Chicago.

This week, I had the honor of spending time with Lincoln and Parker Moss, and their truly amazing mom Kelly.  They drove from Salem to our nation’s Capitol to tell me about their beloved brother and son, Weston Moss.

Weston was 12. A proud Boy Scout. Loved Super Mario and Legos. Dreamed of designing games at Nintendo. He was an artist who shared his beautiful art with the world.

For his 11th birthday, Weston skipped presents and instead donated 500 LEGO sets to kids fighting cancer at the Jimmy Fund Clinic.

Even while battling a rare bone cancer called Ewing Sarcoma, Wes never stopped thinking of other kids in the fight. In his final days, he had one more wish: that we carry on his mission of ending cancer as we know it and making life better for everyone one of us who is blessed to be living it. 

That’s how Weston’s Big Wish was born.

This morning, I was in Salem with Weston’s amazingly resilient dad James and his loving grandmother Donna at the Salem Lions Race Against Childhood Cancer — neighbors, some meeting the Moss family for the first time, showing up for a truly remarkable boy who gave his all to others.

That’s the living legacy and blessed soul of Weston Moss. That’s Salem. That’s New Hampshire. 

I will never stop fighting to make Weston’s Big Wish a reality: more federal funding for research, kinder treatments, and more joy for every kid facing what Wes faced.

May God bless Weston Moss and the entire Moss family.​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​ 🙏

Nike and Converse, what the hell were you thinking?

Your campaign shows what looks like a hooded Klansman, framed by what appears to be the dangling feet of a lynching victim. There is nothing creative or artistic about it. It is racist, reckless and deeply offensive.

I am a Black man, a son of the South and a Member of Congress from Louisiana. Where I come from, the image of Black people hanging from trees is not ancient history. That pain still lives in our families and communities. The white hood is not some harmless costume. It is a symbol of terror, murder and generations of racial violence.

Do not insult our intelligence by dismissing this as an unfortunate misunderstanding. An advertising campaign does not just appear. It is conceived, photographed, reviewed, approved and distributed. At every stage, someone had the opportunity—and the responsibility—to say no.

Who created this campaign? Who approved it? How many executives saw it? Were there any Black people in the room? If so, did anyone listen to them?

You do not get to quietly pull the images, issue a polished apology and move on. You do not get a do-over. The public deserves to know how this happened, who was responsible and what you intend to do about it.

Black pain is not a marketing prop. Lynching is not a creative concept. The Ku Klux Klan is not an aesthetic.

This campaign should never have been created, approved or released. Nike and Converse must answer for it. You have caused real harm, and repairing that harm will require more than an apology written by your public relations department.

@Nike @converse @blackcaucus @USProgressives @HouseDemocrats @MSNOWNews @NAACP_LDF @NAACP @TheRevAl
